learning_science.principle: Manipulatives externalize the viewpoint computation and lower working-memory load
learning_science.why: Sliding a real screen lets a child test the line of sight instead of holding it in mind, widening who can demonstrate the skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use draggable snap-to screens and objects with a live sight-ray so exploration is cheap and only the visibility decision is scored.
learning_science.source: Kirsh, D., & Maglio, P. (1994). On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science, 18(4), 513-549.

tail_precision_rationale: First-action latency (M-RTFIRST) and exploration (M-EXPLORE: screen positions tried) separate children who see the sight-line at a glance from those who slide-and-check; on hard multi-seeker items where a spot must be hidden from several viewpoints at once (high M-DIFFREACH), placing the block correctly on the first move along an efficient path (M-EFF, M-PATH) marks a child who computes several lines of sight simultaneously, a perspective signal beyond right or wrong.
age_rationale: Level-1 visibility judgments are reliable from about age 3, so the type starts at K-1 with one seeker and one screen slot; 2-3 adds more slots and a movable toy; 4-5 uses several seekers who must all be blocked (or a spot visible to exactly one). It stops at 4-5 because older bands are better served by the harder Level-2 appearance types (SPA-VIEW-01, SPA-SCENE-01, SPA-ROADMAP-01); large snap targets keep motor demand minimal.

adaptive.content_range: one seeker, one screen slot, block the view (K-1) to hiding a toy from several seekers at once or revealing it to exactly one (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of seekers; number of screen and target snap positions; block-all versus reveal-to-one; scene clutter; obliqueness of the sight-line
adaptive.notes: Seeker, target, and obstacle coordinates are sampled and each line-of-sight is computed by segment intersection, so items and the block/clear key clone automatically.

engagement_hook: A playful hide-and-seek: slide the fort wall to hide the treasure from the pirate's gaze, with the sight-beam snapping red the instant the view is blocked.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap-to slots, large drag targets); reading (fully wordless, icon seekers); developmental floor avoided by scoring Level-1 visibility rather than Level-2 appearance; mistaking a partially blocked ray for blocked (require full occlusion within tolerance and show ray color clearly).

name: Snap the Photo
one_liner: A camera-character sits on one side of a small scene and the child taps which of several photos shows exactly what that character sees.
interaction: A scene of a few distinct objects is shown from above with a camera-character on one side. Below are three or four candidate photos (front-on views); the child taps the photo matching what the camera sees from its side, then taps LOCK. Distractor photos include the child's own (opposite) view, a left-right mirrored view, and a neighbour-side view. For older bands the camera sits at diagonal positions and more objects are added. In warm-up the chosen photo is checked against a live preview; in scored items the preview is hidden.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand moves the camera to one side, a thought-bubble shows its photo, and the matching option lights green with a chime; one warm-up (two objects, two photos) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Level-2 perspective taking is measurable by recognition before it can be produced
learning_science.why: Children can pick the correct appearance of a scene from another viewpoint earlier than they can generate it, so a photo-choice format extends viewpoint reasoning down to K-1.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a forced choice among photos (recognition) rather than asking the child to build the view, and include an egocentric own-view foil to detect residual self-centering.
learning_science.source: Masangkay, Z. S., McCluskey, K. A., McIntyre, C. W., Sims-Knight, J., Vaughn, B. E., & Flavell, J. H. (1974). The early development of inferences about the visual percepts of others. Child Development, 45(2), 357-366.

learning_science.principle: Designed distractors turn errors into diagnostic information
learning_science.why: An egocentric (opposite-view) foil, a mirror foil, and a neighbour-side foil each reveal a different failure of the viewpoint transformation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Tag each distractor by its error class and log which the child picks so near-misses are typed rather than pooled.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov, M., & Hegarty, M. (2001). A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability. Memory & Cognition, 29(5), 745-756.

tail_precision_rationale: Because the response is one tap, reaction time (M-RT) and error typing (M-ERRTYPE: choosing the opposite own-view is an egocentric near-miss versus a random pick) come out clean; at the tail, correct photo choices from opposite and diagonal camera positions (high M-DIFFREACH) with few option revisits (M-EXPLORE) and well-calibrated confidence (M-CONF) mark a child with a true allocentric model rather than one reading off their own view.
age_rationale: Recognizing another's view is accessible earlier than generating it, so K-1 uses two objects, a side camera, and two photos with an obvious egocentric foil; 2-3 adds objects and a third photo; 4-5 uses opposite and diagonal camera positions with mirror and neighbour-side foils. Tapping a large photo removes motor demand; the type stops at 4-5 because the generative SPA-VIEW-01 and SPA-SCENE-01 types carry the harder 6-8 work.

adaptive.content_range: two objects, side camera, two photos (K-1) to four objects at diagonal or opposite positions with mirror and neighbour foils (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; camera offset (side/opposite/diagonal); number of photo options; distractor classes (egocentric/mirror/neighbour); object distinctiveness
adaptive.notes: Objects are placed at coordinates and each candidate photo is rendered by projecting onto a viewpoint's left-right axis, so the key and the typed distractors clone automatically.

engagement_hook: A photo-booth game: peek through the camera-critter's lens and pick its snapshot, with a shutter-click and green frame when you match its view.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading (icons, no words); motor (large tappable photos); developmental floor (recognition format plus egocentric-foil scoring, report reliability at K-1); guessing (three or more options at older bands and a confidence check); left-right mirror confusion typed separately via M-ERRTYPE.

name: What Is It Looking At?
one_liner: A character faces into a ring of objects and the child taps the object directly in its line of sight, or for older bands turns the character to aim at a named target.
interaction: A character token faces a direction inside a ring of objects. For younger bands the child taps the object the character is looking straight at (the one on its forward heading); a forward gaze-arrow is shown in warm-up only. For older bands the child drags to rotate the character (snapping to detents) so it faces a named target, then taps LOCK, and the set heading is scored against the true bearing. Objects are icons so no reading is required.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand shows the character's gaze-arrow sweeping onto an object that lights green with a chime, then the arrow hides and the child taps; one warm-up (three objects, gaze shown) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Computing another agent's line of sight (gaze) is a foundational perspective-taking ability present early
learning_science.why: Inferring where an agent is looking along its forward heading is an early-developing social-spatial skill, valid at K-1, before appearance-based Level-2 reasoning is reliable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: At young bands ask the child to identify the object on the character's forward heading, a direct line-of-sight judgment scored as accuracy.
learning_science.source: Flavell, J. H., Everett, B. A., Croft, K., & Flavell, E. R. (1981). Young children's knowledge about visual perception: Further evidence for the Level 1-Level 2 distinction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 73(1), 99-103.

learning_science.principle: Continuous heading error grades perspective responses more finely than right or wrong
learning_science.why: Turning a character to face a target yields a signed angular error whose systematic part indexes residual egocentric bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: At older bands score the heading the child sets against the true bearing (M-VIEWANG) rather than a discrete pick.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov, M., & Hegarty, M. (2001). A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability. Memory & Cognition, 29(5), 745-756.

tail_precision_rationale: At young bands, error typing (M-ERRTYPE: tapping the object nearest the child rather than the one on the character's heading is egocentric versus random) separates viewpoint reasoning from proximity guessing; at older bands continuous heading error (M-VIEWANG) grades the top precisely, and low angular error when the character faces away from the child (high M-DIFFREACH) marks a true allocentric heading model.
age_rationale: Identifying where a character looks is accessible at K-1 (tap the object on its forward heading); 2-3 adds more objects and off-centre headings; 4-5 switches to turning the character to face a named target, scored by continuous angular error. Snap detents and large tap targets keep motor demand low. It stops at 4-5 because the 6-8 heading work is carried by SPA-VIEW-01's pointing dial.

adaptive.content_range: tap the object a character looks straight at among three (K-1) to rotating the character to face a named target scored by angular error (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; angular spacing; forward-tap versus rotate-to-face; heading offset from the child's own view; detent granularity
adaptive.notes: Objects on a ring and the character heading are parameterized, so the on-heading object and the true bearing for angular scoring are computed for every clone; works_well is med because allocentric heading onset is mid-childhood.

engagement_hook: A follow-the-look game: spot exactly what the puppy is staring at, then grow up to spin it to eye a hidden treat, with a warm chime when your aim is true.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (Level-1 gaze at young bands, angular at older; report reliability); motor (large taps, snap detents); egocentric proximity confound typed via M-ERRTYPE; reading (icons only).

name: Fold to Shape
one_liner: The child folds a square sheet along a shown crease and predicts the outline the paper makes after folding, by choosing or building the resulting silhouette.
interaction: A square sheet with a dotted crease and a fold arrow is shown. The child scrubs a fold slider (or taps FOLD) to animate the flap folding over; to answer, the child taps which of several silhouettes matches the folded outline (younger bands) or drags the folded edges onto a grid to reproduce the shape (older). One fold at K-1, two orthogonal folds at 2-3, a diagonal fold at 4-5. In warm-up the fold completes and the true outline is shown; in scored items the child commits the silhouette first, then taps LOCK.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand pushes the fold slider so a corner folds over and the square becomes a smaller shape that matches one silhouette with a chime; one warm-up (single straight fold) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Dynamic forward mental folding is achievable by young children and precedes the harder unfolding skill
learning_science.why: Predicting the shape after folding a sheet is within reach at K-1, unlike reasoning back from an unfolded punched pattern.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ask for the resulting outline after a forward fold (not the reverse), starting at K-1 with a single fold.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

learning_science.principle: Surface development and folding is a canonical spatial-visualization (VZ) marker
learning_science.why: Mapping a folded configuration is a core visualization operation on the space factor.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an actual fold animation the child controls plus a silhouette choice so the score reflects the folded result.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, R. B., French, J. W., Harman, H. H., & Dermen, D. (1976). Manual for Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests. Educational Testing Service, Paper Folding (VZ-2).

tail_precision_rationale: Graded silhouette overlap (M-POLY) and error typing (M-ERRTYPE: right number of layers but wrong fold direction is a systematic near-miss versus random) extract tail information from one item; the sharpest separator is accuracy on two-fold and diagonal-fold items (high M-DIFFREACH) where the outline depends on tracking several edges at once.
age_rationale: Forward folding of a single crease is accessible at K-1, so K-1 uses one straight fold and a silhouette choice; 2-3 uses two orthogonal folds; 4-5 adds a diagonal fold and a build-the-outline response. K-1 is included because the task is forward (predict the folded shape), not the reversal reasoning that pushes SPA-PUNCH-01 and SPA-FOLDNET-01 to 2-3 and up. Large taps and snap edges keep motor demand minimal.

adaptive.content_range: single straight fold, pick the silhouette (K-1) to a diagonal fold with a build-the-outline response (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of folds; fold orientation (orthogonal versus diagonal); pick-silhouette versus build-outline; decorated-face tracking; number of options
adaptive.notes: A fold sequence over a square defines the item; the folded outline is computed by reflecting the sheet polygon across each crease, so silhouettes and the key clone automatically and overlap is exact.

engagement_hook: Satisfying fold-the-paper-and-watch-its-shape-change play, with the folded outline snapping to match a silhouette like closing a pop-up card.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (slider scrub or taps, snap edges); giving away the answer (reveal only in warm-up or after commit); ambiguous silhouettes (generate a unique folded outline, verify); confusing decorated-face orientation with shape (score outline shape, keep decoration as an optional harder layer).

name: Butterfly Fold
one_liner: Half of a symmetric picture is painted on a sheet; the child folds it over the crease and predicts where the paint prints onto the blank half, completing the mirror-symmetric picture.
interaction: A sheet shows a dotted centre crease with coloured marks on one half. The child scrubs or taps the fold so the painted half folds onto the blank half; because the paint transfers, each mark prints at its mirror position across the crease. To answer, the child taps the blank-half cells where paint will land (and doubled cells where a print meets an existing mark for two-crease items), then taps CHECK. A vertical crease at K-1, then horizontal and diagonal creases, and a second fold for 6-8. Warm-up folds and reveals the print; scored items commit first.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand folds the painted half over and the marks stamp mirror-images onto the far half with a soft print sound; one warm-up (one mark, vertical crease) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Reflective symmetry is perceptually salient and usable by young children
learning_science.why: Symmetry about a vertical axis is detected and completed early, making a fold-to-mirror task valid at K-1.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Start with a vertical crease (the most salient symmetry axis) and score the reflected print.
learning_science.source: Bornstein, M. H., Ferdinandsen, K., & Gross, C. G. (1981). Perception of symmetry in infancy. Developmental Psychology, 17(1), 82-86.

learning_science.principle: Mental folding that maps marks across a crease is a reflective transformation distinct from rotation
learning_science.why: Applying an axis reflection to predict where features superimpose is its own visualization operation with its own developmental trajectory.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the predicted print against the reflected union of marks and type wrong-axis near-misses.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

tail_precision_rationale: Graded overlap of predicted versus true print (M-POLY) and error typing (M-ERRTYPE: reflected across the wrong axis versus random) grade responses finely; at the tail, accuracy on diagonal-axis and two-crease prints (high M-DIFFREACH) with little scrubbing (M-EXPLORE) marks a child who applies the reflection internally rather than by trial.
age_rationale: Vertical-axis symmetry completion is accessible at K-1; 2-3 adds horizontal axes and more marks; 4-5 adds diagonal axes and doubled overlaps; 6-8 uses two creases in sequence. K-1 is included because completing a mirror is easier than reversing folds. Large snap cells keep motor demand minimal, and warm-up reveals the print to teach the rule.

adaptive.content_range: one mark, vertical crease (K-1) to two-crease diagonal prints with doubled overlaps (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: axis orientation (vertical/horizontal/diagonal); number of marks; single versus double crease; doubled-overlap cells; grid resolution
adaptive.notes: Marks and creases are parameterized and the print is the reflected union across each crease, so every clone is auto-keyed and partial credit is exact.

engagement_hook: Like the classic fold-the-painted-paper-into-a-butterfly craft: press the halves together and watch the pattern mirror itself into a whole.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large snap cells); giving away the rule (reveal only in warm-up); axis ambiguity (draw the crease boldly); confusing single versus doubled marks (distinct doubled-cell colour, score both).

name: Which Fold Made It?
one_liner: Shown a paper before and after a single fold, the child works out which crease and direction produced the result by choosing or performing the fold.
interaction: The top shows a decorated square (before) and its folded result (after). Below are candidate fold lines (dotted) with direction arrows; the child taps the one crease-and-direction that turns the before into the after, then taps LOCK. An alternate do-it shell lets the child draw the crease by dragging between two edges and pick a direction, animating to check. Younger bands offer two or three horizontal or vertical creases; older bands add diagonal creases and off-centre folds. A REPLAY of the after-shape counts as a scaffold.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand taps a candidate crease and the before-paper folds along it into the after-shape with a chime, while a wrong crease folds to a different shape; one warm-up (two candidate creases) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Selecting the transformation that produced a result (not just predicting a result) taxes and reveals the internal fold model more fully
learning_science.why: Reasoning backward from a result to its cause is a distinct, more diagnostic demand than forward prediction (generation effect).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Make the response the fold that produced the result (an inverse task) scored against the unique crease-and-direction.
learning_science.source: Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4(6), 592-604.

learning_science.principle: Forward mental folding underlies the inverse judgment and is available in early childhood
learning_science.why: Matching a fold to its outcome relies on the same dynamic folding representation young children already possess.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep single folds and concrete before/after images so K-1 children can reason about the crease.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

tail_precision_rationale: Replay-scaffold use (M-HINT) and candidates sampled (M-EXPLORE) show whether the child infers the crease at a glance or hunts; error typing (M-ERRTYPE: correct crease line but wrong fold direction versus a wrong line) plus first-try accuracy on diagonal and off-centre folds with no replays (high M-DIFFREACH, zero M-HINT) is an inverse-folding tail signal.
age_rationale: With concrete before/after pictures and single folds, matching a fold to its result is accessible at K-1 (two candidate creases); 2-3 adds a third candidate and a direction; 4-5 adds diagonal and off-centre creases. K-1 is included because single-fold reasoning with a visible outcome is within reach; large taps keep motor demand low. It caps at 4-5 since multi-fold reversal lives in SPA-PUNCH-01 and SPA-FOLDOVER-01 at higher bands.

adaptive.content_range: two candidate creases, straight fold (K-1) to diagonal and off-centre creases with direction (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of candidate creases; crease orientation; fold direction included; off-centre folds; replay availability
adaptive.notes: The before polygon, crease, and direction determine the after polygon; distractor creases produce distinct after-shapes, so the unique key clones automatically.

engagement_hook: A reverse-engineer-the-fold puzzle: figure out the secret crease that turned the flat paper into the shape, then watch it fold to confirm.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large tappable creases); over-reliance on replay (counted via M-HINT); ambiguous folds (ensure exactly one crease-and-direction yields the after-shape); reading (icons and arrows only).

name: Builder's Studio
one_liner: The child builds a model by placing and rotating blocks on a snap grid, matching a target blueprint on scored trials and freely inventing a creation in an open build.
interaction: A palette of blocks (squares, rectangles, and ramps at K-1; unit cubes on an isometric board at older bands) feeds a snap grid. The child drags a block in, taps to rotate it (snaps 90 degrees), and it locks to the nearest cell or voxel; undo and clear are available. Scored trials show a target (a 2D pattern, or for 6-8 orthographic front/side/top views) and score the per-cell match; a final open build-anything trial has an always-visible DONE and no target, logging what the child chooses to make.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drags a block in, rotates it once to match the target, and snaps it green; one warm-up (place two blocks, no rotation) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Block construction predicts and builds the spatial skills linked to mathematics and STEM
learning_science.why: Assembling structures to a model taps part-whole visualization that forecasts later achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use build-to-target trials scored per cell or voxel plus an open build, spanning copy and creation.
learning_science.source: Verdine, B. N., Golinkoff, R. M., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Newcombe, N. S., Filipowicz, A. T., & Chang, A. (2014). Deconstructing building blocks: Preschoolers' spatial assembly performance relates to early mathematical skills. Child Development, 85(3), 1062-1076.

learning_science.principle: Orienting each piece to fit requires mental rotation
learning_science.why: Turning a block to the needed orientation before placing is an analog rotation, so building exercises rotation as well as assembly.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require rotation to complete targets and log rotations and their efficiency as a process signal.
learning_science.source: Shepard, R. N., & Metzler, J. (1971). Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects. Science, 171(3972), 701-703.

learning_science.principle: Open creative production reveals divergent, creative-productive giftedness that keyed items miss
learning_science.why: A free build scored for fluency, originality, and elaboration captures the creativity ring of giftedness and authentic construction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a no-target free build and score it with an anchored consensual rubric plus idea fluency and originality.
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: Per-cell partial credit (M-POLY) with build trajectory (M-PROG) and rotation/placement efficiency (M-EFF, M-PATH, low M-REV) expose whether a child decomposes a target and places each block in near-minimal moves; reproducing a hard blueprint (high M-DIFFREACH) plus, on the open build, idea fluency, originality, elaboration and rubric quality (M-IDEAFLU, M-ORIG, M-ELAB, M-RUBRIC) with free-choice engagement (M-CHOICE) add a creative-productive axis CogAT lacks, jointly grading the analytic and creative tails.
age_rationale: Snapping blocks into a grid makes construction accessible at K-1 (two or three large solid blocks, no rotation); 2-3 adds 90-degree rotation; 4-5 uses larger 2D targets; 6-8 builds 3D voxel models to orthographic blueprints. Snap-to cells and voxels remove placement dexterity so scores reflect analysis, rotation, and invention rather than aim.

adaptive.content_range: place two or three blocks to copy a simple shape and free-build (K-1) to building a 3D voxel model to front/side/top views plus an open creation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: 2D versus 3D; block count and shape variety; rotation required; blueprint versus orthographic views; open versus targeted; palette size
adaptive.notes: Targets are sampled block-and-rotation per cell (or voxel sets rendered to three views), so unlimited matched build-to-target clones exist; the open build is scored by rubric and fluency, not a key.

engagement_hook: A Lego-like studio: snap and spin blocks to nail the blueprint, then a free build-anything round where your creation is celebrated, with the pull of just one more piece.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap cells and voxels, large blocks); rotation discoverability (ghost-hand shows the rotate tap); open-build scoring subjectivity (anchored rubric plus multiple raters for M-RUBRIC, automatic fluency and originality counts); colour vision (distinguish blocks by shape and pattern, not hue only); device screen size for 3D boards (generous cells, scrollable).

name: Marble Run Maker
one_liner: The child places and tilts ramps, funnels, and chutes so a dropped marble rolls from the start to the goal, and in harder items collects required stars along the way.
interaction: A board has a fixed marble drop-start and a goal bucket. The child drags track pieces (straight ramps, bends, funnels; catchers for older bands) from a tray onto snap slots and taps to flip or tilt their slope; pressing PLAY drops the marble and it rolls under a simple gravity model along the placed pieces. The run succeeds when the marble reaches the goal; route-planning items add required stars the path must hit and a fewest-pieces target. An open make-your-own-run trial logs free creation, and retry is always available.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drops a ramp into a slot, tilts it toward the goal, and the marble rolls down and into the bucket with a chime; one warm-up (one ramp bridges start to goal) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Constructing a working path to a goal is look-ahead planning and constraint satisfaction
learning_science.why: Arranging pieces so the marble reaches the goal requires simulating the route and satisfying connectivity, a planning demand.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require a working start-to-goal run (with required stars for harder items) scored against a fewest-pieces optimum, not just success.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 298(1089), 199-209.

learning_science.principle: Physical construction play develops spatial reasoning and predicts STEM learning
learning_science.why: Building functional structures engages and strengthens the spatial skills tied to later achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a hands-on build-and-test contraption with an open creative round scored for originality and fluency of working solutions.
learning_science.source: Wai, J., Lubinski, D., & Benbow, C. P. (2009). Spatial ability for STEM domains: Aligning over 50 years of cumulative psychological knowledge. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(4), 817-835.

learning_science.principle: Predicting how each sloped piece redirects the marble is spatial visualization of trajectories
learning_science.why: Judging where a ball exits a tilted ramp couples orientation with mental simulation of motion.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use rotatable slope pieces and log rotations and test-runs as process signals.
learning_science.source: Hegarty, M. (2004). Dynamic visualizations and learning: Getting to the difficult questions. Learning and Instruction, 14(3), 343-351.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial credit for path progress and stars reached (M-POLY), placement efficiency versus the fewest-pieces optimum (M-EFF), and test-run exploration (M-EXPLORE, M-PATH) reveal whether a child plans the whole run or tinkers piece-by-piece (high M-REV); solving a dense multi-star run in near-minimal pieces (high M-DIFFREACH) plus originality, fluency, and rubric quality on the open run (M-IDEAFLU, M-ORIG, M-RUBRIC, M-CHOICE) grade the planning and creative-construction tails together.
age_rationale: With snap slots and one required piece, bridging start to goal is accessible at K-1; 2-3 uses a few ramps and bends; 4-5 adds funnels and one required star; 6-8 uses dense boards with several stars and a fewest-pieces target. Snap-to placement and tap-to-tilt remove dexterity so success reflects route planning and construction, not fine motor control.

adaptive.content_range: one ramp bridges start to goal (K-1) to a dense multi-star run under a fewest-pieces target plus an open build (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: board size; piece variety (ramps/bends/funnels/catchers); number of required stars; fewest-pieces target; number of decoy slots; open versus targeted
adaptive.notes: A solvable board is generated from a known working run then pieces are scrambled or removed, so the fewest-pieces optimum and star key are computed for every clone; the marble path is deterministic under the simple gravity model.

engagement_hook: The irresistible marble-run tinkerer: tilt the ramps, hit PLAY, and cheer as the marble rattles down and plops into the bucket, with beg-to-retry fun.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap slots, tap-to-tilt, large pieces); rewarding blind tinkering (credit efficiency M-EFF and plan-first latency M-RTFIRST, not test-run count); multiple valid runs (score connectivity, stars, and piece efficiency, accept any working run); frustration on failure (unlimited retries, encouraging feedback, and M-CHOICE gauges voluntary persistence).

name: Program the Bot
one_liner: The child assembles a short sequence of move commands (a little program) that drives a robot across a grid to the goal, collecting required gems in the fewest steps.
interaction: A grid shows a robot at start, a goal, walls, and (harder) gems. The child builds a command strip by tapping or dragging arrow tiles (up/down/left/right for young bands, forward/turn for older) into an ordered sequence, then presses RUN to watch the robot execute it step by step, stopping if it hits a wall. The child edits the sequence and re-runs until the robot reaches the goal with all gems. Older bands add a step budget, a turn-relative command set, and a repeat/loop tile for simple scripting.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drops three arrow tiles into the strip and presses RUN; the robot steps along them to the goal with a chime; one warm-up (two steps, straight line) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Sequencing move commands to reach a goal is look-ahead route planning
learning_science.why: Composing an ordered plan the robot executes requires simulating the whole route before acting, a planning demand beyond step-by-step tracing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the program against a fewest-steps optimum and the required-gem key, not just arrival.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 298(1089), 199-209.

learning_science.principle: Early programming and robotics build sequencing and computational thinking accessible to young children
learning_science.why: Command-sequence tools such as programmable floor robots are used successfully from kindergarten, so a build-a-program route task is valid at K-1.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use tangible arrow tiles and a visible run so K-1 children compose and test a short sequence, adding a loop tile only for older bands.
learning_science.source: Bers, M. U. (2018). Coding as a Playground: Programming and Computational Thinking in the Early Childhood Classroom. New York: Routledge.

tail_precision_rationale: Program length versus the fewest-steps optimum (M-EFF), the command sequence (M-PATH), plan-first latency (M-RTFIRST), and edits and re-runs (M-REV, M-HINT run-and-test uses) reveal whether the child plans the full route or edits reactively; recovering after a crash (M-RESUME) and solving dense multi-gem grids in near-optimal programs on few runs (high M-DIFFREACH) is a plan-and-debug tail signature, while M-PROG tracks partial route completion across runs.
age_rationale: Composing a two or three command sequence with absolute arrows and a visible run is accessible at K-1 (programmable floor robots are used in kindergarten); 2-3 lengthens sequences and adds walls; 4-5 adds gems and a step budget; 6-8 uses turn-relative commands and a repeat/loop tile. Tapping arrow tiles removes fine-motor demand so the score reflects planning, not dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: two or three absolute-arrow steps to the goal (K-1) to turn-relative programs with loops, gems, and a step budget on a dense grid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size and walls; sequence length; absolute versus turn-relative commands; number of gems; step budget; loop tile enabled
adaptive.notes: A grid, walls, and gem set define the item; the fewest-steps program is computed by shortest-path search, so the optimum and key clone automatically; the robot's execution is deterministic.

engagement_hook: A beloved code-the-robot game: line up the arrows, hit RUN, and watch your little bot march to the treasure, tweaking and re-running until it nails the path.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (tap or drag large arrow tiles); reading (icon arrows, no text); rewarding trial-and-error over planning (credit program efficiency M-EFF and plan-first latency, count re-runs via M-HINT); left-right or turn-relative confusion at young bands (use absolute arrows until 6-8); frustration (unlimited edits and re-runs, M-RESUME gauges recovery not penalty).
